That seems like a promising pattern to verify against the remaining example.

Maybe the marked edge relates to the longest contiguous straight segment, but that doesn't quite line up either. Let me try comparing the center of mass against the bounding box center instead — perhaps the marked edge is the direction the shape is skewed away from, so in ex1 the mass sits left of center, suggesting the opposite edge gets marked.

That doesn't fit either. Let me try tracing each shape as a path instead: in ex1 the line runs top to bottom with a branch extending right, so that branch points toward the right wall. In ex3 the branches extend upward from the main horizontal line, pointing toward the top. In ex2 the main line runs horizontally with a branch extending toward one side too—so maybe the marked edge is wherever a branch sticks out from the main path.

Checking against ex2 and ex3 breaks the right/left pattern I tried, so I'm testing another idea: maybe the marked edge is simply the farthest one from the shape's bulk, which fits ex2 and ex3 but not ex1. I'm now considering whether the direction relates to the shape's endpoints or "tips" instead—looking at where the degree-1 cells point in ex2 to see if a majority direction emerges.

Let me try counting filled cells across examples to see if the total maps to a direction: 22, 16, 20 for the three cases, checking if these correspond to top/right/bottom somehow via mod 4.

Instead I'm tracing the actual shapes: in example 1 there's a thick vertical line with a horizontal spike sticking out to the right at row 3, suggesting the unique protrusion determines which wall it points toward. In example 3 I'm looking for a similar protrusion, like a vertical extension going upward from column 6.

But example 2 breaks the pattern — the spike there points downward yet the marked wall is the top, which seems inconsistent with example 3 where an upward spike also matches the top wall. I'm trying to figure out if maybe I'm misreading which segment counts as the "spike" versus the main body of the shape.

So I switch to testing whether the marked edge instead corresponds to the largest or smallest empty region bordering the shape, computing gap sizes on each side across the examples to see if that's the actual rule.

Since gap size doesn't hold for ex1 (largest is left, not the marked right), I try a different theory: the marked edge matches the direction of the shape's longest straight segment, checking whether that segment's free end points toward the marked side in each example.

But re-examining ex2's row data, col2 spans rows7-11 with the free end at bottom, which contradicts my rule again — so ex2 remains inconsistent with this theory and I need to recheck the actual row structure more carefully.

Maybe I'm wrong about which edge to mark; perhaps it's not about proximity to grid edges but about the shape's own directionality — like the tail-to-head vector of the line, or which end is "thinner" versus "wider" in the overall path.

Let me test another angle: maybe whichever axis has the larger span dictates the marked edge — vertical-dominant shapes mark the right edge, horizontal-dominant shapes mark the top edge. Checking all three examples this pattern holds consistently, so that could be the actual rule.

But I realize I don't actually have the test input in front of me to apply this rule to — I need to wait until it's provided before I can submit a prediction.
